previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%), atrial fibrillation, restrictive lung disease, and chronic kidney disease was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and chest pressure over two days, associated with URI symptoms. Initial evaluation revealed acute on chronic kidney injury (creatinine 2.2, baseline 1.5), likely prerenal from mild heart failure, and elevated BNP of 650. He was treated with nebulizers and a short course of prednisone for reactive airway disease in the setting of a viral upper respiratory infection. Antibiotics were discontinued after clarification that he does not have COPD. His kidney function initially improved with diuresis but worsened to 2.7 due to over-diuresis; it subsequently improved to 2.3 with holding torsemide and IV fluids. He was discharged home with stable vital signs, instructions to follow up with his PCP for labs and medication management, pulmonology for ongoing lung evaluation, and a scheduled CT for a known pulmonary nodule. Amiodarone was continued, but concern for its pulmonary effects was communicated to cardiology.
problems: Acute upper respiratory infections of unspecified site
Acute on chronic systolic heart failure
Automatic implantable cardiac defibrillator in situ
Other diseases of lung, not elsewhere classified
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, uncontrolled

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old male with history of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy EF 
20%, restrictive lung disease,  left upper lobe nodule c/w early 
stage lung cancer s/p cyberknnife radiation therapy completed 
___ and untreated severe mixed sleep apnea with obstruction 
presents with 2 days of worsening shortness of breath.

#Shortness of Breath: Seems pulmonary in origin, rather than 
cardiac given lack of edema, dry CXR, and BNP that is at his 
baseline. In addition, his weight is down 5 lb from ___. His crackles and rhonchi are more consistent with COPD 
and/or ILD. His CT imaging reveals bilateral ground glass 
opacities and reticulation
which may represent an early interstitial lung disease. He has 
been on amiodarone for years and this could represent amiodarone 
pulmonary toxicity. Discontinuing amiodarone can be considered, 
pending discussion with his outpatient cardiologist. He also has 
asbestos pleural disease and this may represent early 
parenchymal disease. His prior PFT's suggest a bit of a mixed 
picture of restrictive and obstructive disease. Given this, we 
continued his albuterol rescue inhaler and started tiotropium 
once daily. His orthopnea may be secondary to untreated severe 
sleep apnea noted on sleep study in ___. He was trialed on 
CPAP 10 cm H2O with 2L bleed through and tolerated this well.  
He is amenable to using CPAP at home but will need repeat sleep 
study in order for this to be covered by insurance. We will 
arrange follow up with Dr. ___ in sleep clinic. In the setting 
of his severe apnea and underlying reflux he may also be 
experiencing laryngospasm. Per pulmonology, his exam does not 
reveal paradoximal breathing to suggest diaphragmatic
dysfunction, but he may benefit from further evaluation with 
upright and supine spirometry as well as MIP/MEP testing. We 
will also arrange follow-up in Pulmonary clinic with a full set 
of PFTs. Per pulmonology, he may also benefit from high 
resolution supine and prone CT chest. He felt that his breathing 
was much improved at the time of discharge; the only 
interventions were albuterol and ipratroprium nebs, CPAP and 
brief smoking cessation. He was strongly encouraged to quit 
smoking, but is not ready to set a quit date.  He declined 
nicotine patches (states that they do not work), gum and 
lozenges.
.

imipramine/mirtazapine/perphenazine.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Shortness of breath, CHF, assess for pulmonary edema or
effusions.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to multiple prior chest radiographs, most
recently dated ___ and a CT chest performed ___.

FINDINGS:  Frontal and lateral chest radiographs demonstrate stable severe
cardiomegaly.  Mediastinal and hilar contours are unremarkable.  Defibrillator
lead is positioned in the right ventricle.  On a background of emphysema and
chronic lung changes, there are bibasilar reticular and linear opacifications,
likely reflecting superimposed atelectasis in the setting of low lung volumes.
No overt pulmonary edema evident.  No pleural effusions.

IMPRESSION:  Stable severe cardiomegaly.  Faint bibasilar opacifications on
background emphysema and chronic lung disease likely reflect atelectasis.  No
overt pulmonary edema.

EXAMINATION:  CT CHEST W/O CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with restrictive lung disease. Assess for
progression of ILD (asbestos related changes), prior nodule that had
cyberknife, COPD related changes

TECHNIQUE:  Axial CT images of the chest were obtained with intravenous
contrast . Sagittal and coronal reformats were obtained.

DLP: 690 mGy-cm

COMPARISON:  CT ___, and ___.

FINDINGS: 

Pacemaker leads are again noted in the right atrium and right ventricle. There
is minor atheromatous calcification involving the thoracic aorta. The heart
size is normal. Coronary artery calcification is noted. 9 mm right pre-carinal
lymph node is unchanged from the prior examination. There is no hilar
lymphadenopathy. 6 mm calcified left thyroid nodule is unchanged.

Bilateral calcified and noncalcified pleural plaques are again noted in
keeping with asbestos related pleural disease. Several nodular areas of
pleural thickening in the right middle lobe (series 4, image 106 and 133), and
right lower lobe (series 4 image 155) are unchanged from prior examinations
dating back to ___. There is moderate centrilobular and paraseptal emphysema
similar in appearance to the prior examination.

There is a single fiducial seed noted in the lesion along the peripheral
aspect of the left upper lobe/ superior lingula.  The lesion is solid and
spiculated measuring 2.4 x 1.4 cm similar in size to the prior exam.

5 mm fissural nodule along the right minor fissure anteriorly is unchanged.
There is an ovoid region of scarring in the apical segment of the right upper
lobe (series 4, image 47) that has increased in prominence from the prior
exam.  There is a 5 mm nodule in the superior segment of the right lower lobe
that is similar to the prior exam (series 4, image 71) and adjacent 2 mm
pulmonary nodule (series 4, image 75).

Bibasilar dependent ground-glass opacities/reticulation are thought to be on
the basis of atelectasis.  No pleural effusion is demonstrated. No osseous
lesion is demonstrated.

IMPRESSION:


1. Features of asbestos related pleural disease are again noted.
2. Moderate centrilobular/ paraseptal emphysema.
3. Spiculated lesion bordering the left lower lobe/superior segment of the
lingula, with a fiducial seed now noted. The lesion is unchanged in size from
___.
4. Pulmonary nodules measuring 5 mm or less stable from the prior exam. An
area of scarring in the apical segment of the right upper lobe (series 4,
image 48) is more prominent, and attention to this region on followup exams is
recommended.
